items.title: Louis Armstrong Interview, 1960-08-02
items.q: musicians like Bix and Paul Whiteburn and all them people sitting down. They couldn't understand how we played so well together.

ctx.x: Well, I stayed with Oliver a long time. See what I mean? After I stayed with Oliver, we got so wedged in together making duets and musicians like Bix and Paul Whiteburn and all them people sitting down. They couldn't understand how we played so well together. When Joe got ready for a break, I had every note to it. And we just sitting right there and didn't say nothing to each other. That's how well I loved them. When did you start recording? When was the first? With Joe Oliver. About 1922. The same time of the…
When you were talking earlier about your playing with Oliver and Kidore, is there somebody now that's playing with you that you expect in the years to come will move to the forefront?

when he was with Paul Whiteman in 1926 or 1927 when I was at the Sunset in Chicago and after he finished at the Chicago Theater, he'd come up to the Sunset, which closed at 4 o'clock in the morning. Then we'd close the doors and we'd play the things we wanted to play. That's the first time I heard Vicks Baidebeck play piano. But he'd start playing all the things in the mist and all that. See, and that was a boy who was so sincere about his horn. Everybody's raving by the solo, but he never said it by it. That's…
That is a long time. Yeah. If some young people would come to you and ask you, what shall we do? We would like to be jazz musicians. What is the best way?

items.title: Louis Armstrong: Jazz Casual Interview, 1964-07-10
items.q: That's where I used to meet Bix up and down that Mississippi River there on that excursion boat from St. Louis to Davenport. Yeah. And I used to see a little youngster. Yeah. And then we'd start meeting all over the country. And sit down. We had sessions.

ctx.x: But that was really the first thing that I lost the memory.

Well, that was my life. That's all I knew of. Sure. But you have to get with different. Now like when I went with Fletcher Anderson's band in 1924. Well, there was something else. There was Don Richmond. The minute I get up on the stand to join the band, there's a part in front of me. You know, well, I was at least tall. And you get conscious. You know, your mind, as you go along, you've got to get with it. Yeah. So you lose something. But is that all good experience for you as a musician? I enjoy the experience.…

So all this added to your own equipment as a truck. As a truck. Yeah. And I didn't try to do nothing else but blows. And you would advise any youngster today to, I would assume, to have as much experience as a concert?
